Our goal is to support the local art community by installing artworks that enhance safety within public spaces. Working with the Sioux Downtown Association and local businesses, light box display cases will be installed within problematic exterior downtown city sites. These light boxes will display artwork that promote wellness as well as physically lighting up the area, thus creating a safer environment. These will be rotational displays. We will invite various artists to participate through a call for entry, which then enables us to support those artists through creating awareness of their work and providing promotional opportunities for them. Next slide, please. The Bemina Wasaya Light Project will begin in downtown Sioux St. Marie with an ongoing possibility of expansion. After our team conducted a walkthrough of the downtown area, we found numerous potential sites where the light boxes can offer a solution to the city's needs. As in the example, light boxes may be placed in darker alleyways to create a sense of safety and security in the downtown area, lighting the dark places of the city to help find light and hope. Next slide, please. The Bemina Wasaya Lightbox Safety Project directly addresses the current goals of the City of Sioux St. Marie's Community Culture Plan as it ties into the city's need for increased arts and culture, the city's need for communication and connection between community members, various artists and local businesses. It also addresses city downtown activation needs. This project also is a solution to many of the concerns that arose from the 2019 Sioux Downtown Association's walkthrough report, while also complementing the new downtown safety initiative, whose major goal is to decrease crime and violence. Next slide, please. Our research proves that public art helps make communities safer by building community cohesiveness, improving well-being, creating social awareness and positive change, while also decreasing violence and crime. Next slide, please. Other cities are implementing various light-based public art as solutions to similar concerns. Two examples are these neon lights located in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and these illuminated vacant building windows within a revitalization area in Long Beach, California. Next slide, please. The example shown here is from the Blackwood Gallery in Mississauga. The lightbox program exhibits multiple rotating exhibitions that change seasonally, similar to what we are proposing. Next slide. Our proposed lightbox project will allow potential opportunities to display mediums and formats not typically suited to public mural artworks, provide ongoing exhibition space for local artists, exhibit multiple artists at a time, exhibit Algoma University visual art thesis work, and curate exhibitions. Artistic exchange through curated exhibitions will enlarge awareness of Sault Ste. Marie through shared group exhibitions. For example, adding Sault Ste. Marie to artists' CVs, etc. It will expand awareness of local artists into other communities and bring together established and emerging artists. This is a low-cost way to bring in artists from outside our community while putting the city of Sault Ste. Marie at the forefront of various artistic and public forums, as news of the displayed work becomes known. Next slide, please. This project also provides vast potential for building programs such as artist talks and community workshops around the displays, which further engage and build healthy communities. There are also opportunities to partner with other Tourism Ontario, Sault Ste. Marie City, and arts and culture events and programs, such as the Summer Moon Festival, the Downtown Walkaround Tour, Sioux Tourism, the Downtown Revitalization Project, the Community Improvement Plan, and Anishinaabe organizations, just to name a few. Next slide, please. Our initial artist proposal involves a fourth-year visual arts student named Shamaya Nelson. Her digital works involve various Anishinaabe children, which we will display downtown in the Baminawaseya light boxes to portray a sense of hope for the future. In her artist statement, Shamaya states, Ani, hello, my name is Shamaya Nelson and I'm a daughter and granddaughter of residential school survivors of the Pelican Lake Indian Residential School. I've always done my work with an awareness of trying to break the cycle of what happened to my father and grandmother while they were in residential school. I've always expressed my voice through my artwork. I'm trying to strengthen and show the happiness in us again, and to ensure future generations grow up strong and healthy with our culture. For my thesis project, I'm making digital drawings of my son and my niece and nephew, showing the strong, resilient kids that they are and continue to be. I want to bring our culture back that is rightfully ours, to finally be ourselves and to always be ourselves. I want my images to help bring happiness back to our children. They are going to know their grandparents were survivors. I want the children to know they don't have to hide or be scared of who they are. As you can see, Shamaya's work is a great example of this project's potential to make Sault Ste. Marie healthier, happier, and safer. Next slide, please. Our plans are to include a map within our final proposal with the potential multi-phase locations we identified during our downtown walk-around tour, as well as a detailed budget. Our initial phase is to begin with one to four light boxes and high traffic areas with lots of visibility. There are numerous Sioux downtown business owners who are interested in public art, but who are waiting for the right proposal. This project will fill the needs of many of these businesses. Potential donors include Algoma University, City Studio, the City of Sault Ste. Marie, downtown Sioux businesses, and Anishinaabe Arts Associations, to name a few. At this time, we're waiting for the results of the Sewell grant application, which would contribute $4,000 towards the project. Next slide, please. And that is it. We look forward to continuing this project, entitled Beminawaseya, to bring forth new light, while working in conjunction with the City of Sault Ste. Marie and City Studio, as well as Algoma University.
